If FILESYSTEM_DISK is ever switched to 'public' or a public S3 bucket, the files become publicly reachable without any code change.

app/Http/Requests/StoreDocumentRequest.php:12 – string rules 'file','mimes:…','max:5120' instead of the fluent File::types()->max() rule

strengths: Meets every requirement: the probes confirmed MIME detection from file content (an HTML file named .pdf is rejected), randomized hashed storage paths, a 10-minute temporarySignedRoute, 404 via denyAsNotFound for non-owners, and a 404 for a missing file on both link and download
Compact single controller, constrained FK with cascadeOnDelete, the #[Fillable] attribute and a typed HasMany relation
The factory has a sensible user_id default, and a storedDocument helper keeps the tests short
Good test coverage of expiry boundaries (9 vs 11 minutes), bogus signatures, unknown id, guest access and a file that disappears after the link is issued

strengths: Pins the private 'local' disk explicitly for store, exists and download, so confidential files stay private even if the default disk changes

Authorization sits at the route level with ->can('link','document') and a purpose-named policy ability that returns denyAsNotFound

Strongest tests: forgetGuards() proves the download works without login, swapping the id in a signed URL is rejected, the test asserts no files are stored on validation failure, streamedContent is checked, and the stored path is not the client filename
404 on both link and download when the file is missing, and the expiry boundary is tested

v.rationale: Both implementations work and have the same design: a FormRequest with a content-based MIME check, randomized storage paths, a policy that returns denyAsNotFound, a 10-minute temporarySignedRoute to a 'signed' download route, and an exists-check that returns 404 on both link and download. Both suites pass (15 tests each). My probes found no difference in behaviour: a spoofed PDF built from a real file is rejected, a real PDF is accepted, and a tampered `expires` value is rejected. I found no real bugs in either. impl-2 wins on idiom and safety. It names the private 'local' disk explicitly, while impl-1 relies on the default disk, so impl-1 would leak files if FILESYSTEM_DISK changed. impl-2 also uses the fluent File rule, authorizes at the route with a purpose-named ability, and has noticeably stronger tests (a real guest download using forgetGuards, an id-swap tamper test, and a check that nothing reaches disk on validation failure). impl-1 is a little leaner with one controller, but it has an unused Request parameter and its 'download without login' test still runs authenticated.
